title: Blessings on the Prophet ﷺ
hook: Allah and His angels send blessings on the Prophet, so do the same (33:56)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Umm Salamah, and your line was both, equally. Which quality did you notice you share with someone? Day five hundred forty-two.

Look at any page of a Muslim book, a sermon transcript, a social media post about the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. After his name, there's a small curl of Arabic calligraphy, or four letters in brackets, or the words peace be upon him. On this path it's come up again and again, and it can start to feel like punctuation. But it isn't a habit someone invented to be polite. It comes from one verse in the surah we've been reading this week, a verse that says who does it first, before anyone on earth.
screen: `ONE VERSE SAYS WHO DOES IT FIRST.`

segments.voice: Surah Al-Ahzab, verse fifty-six. Pickthall: "Lo! Allah and His angels shower blessings on the Prophet. O ye who believe! Ask blessings on him and salute him with a worthy salutation." Look at the order. First Allah. Then the angels. Only then the believers, asked to join something already happening. The Arabic word is salat, the same word as the daily prayer. Bukhari records an early explanation from Abu al-'Aliya: Allah's salat is His praise of the Prophet before the angels, and the angels' salat is their prayer for him. When believers send it, it's a request: O Allah, bless him. Blessings like these are called salawat, and a common form begins Allahumma salli, O Allah, send blessings. Then there's the small curl you see in print. It stands for sallallahu 'alayhi wa sallam: may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Many Muslims say it aloud or write it when his name comes up. And there's a reason many people count them. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says that whoever sends one blessing on the Prophet, Allah sends ten blessings on that person. One out, ten back. In the daily prayer itself, near the end, Muslims recite a longer salawat, often called the Abrahamic blessing, because it asks that Muhammad and his family be blessed as Ibrahim and his family were blessed. Sunni and Shia Muslims both include the Prophet's family in it; the exact wording varies by school. So the little curl is the end of a long chain: Allah, the angels, and then anyone who reads the name and stops for one breath.
screen: `ALLAH, THEN THE ANGELS, THEN THE BELIEVERS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is ten salawat. Sit, and let your breath slow. If you're Muslim, or want to try, say the short form ten times, quietly, counting on your fingers: Allahumma salli 'ala Muhammad. O Allah, send blessings on Muhammad. If that isn't your practice, sit with the picture from the verse instead: a blessing already moving, from Allah, through the angels, and the invitation to join in. Either way, take the remaining time in silence. The bell holds the time.
Salawat. Blessings on the Prophet ﷺ, what Allah and the angels send first, and what believers ask for, one blessing out and ten returned. Today's word.
Your line: blessings on him. Today, when you see that small curl after his name, or hear peace be upon him, slow down enough to read it as a sentence. Day five hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Muslims say or write sallallahu 'alayhi wa sallam after the Prophet's name, recite the Abrahamic blessing near the end of every prayer, and many count salawat on Fridays or on prayer beads.

original.note: Arabic: may Allah bless him and grant him peace, written in print as ﷺ.

trapdoor: what you thought: a polite phrase after a name.
what it means: an answer to 33:56, joining a blessing that Allah and the angels send first.
what a scholar hears: Abu al-'Aliya, in Bukhari, explains Allah's salat as His praise of the Prophet before the angels and the angels' salat as supplication; the same word names the daily prayer.
